title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting

paper.title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting
paper.abstract:
Abstract. We study the conditional distribution of limit-order volume submitted over
the next five minutes, given the current order book and recent order flow.
The task requires capturing price placement, total volume, and predictive
uncertainty jointly.
Coordinate-wise diffusion losses do not explicitly account for price
displacement, while normalizing fields to unit mass removes information
about total volume. Agreement on selected summary statistics also does not
establish fidelity to the joint field distribution.
We introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for
unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an unbalanced
optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary loss. We also develop a full-field
evaluation framework that combines a transport cost sensitive to price
placement and total volume with proper scoring rules and calibration
diagnostics.
In the primary comparison on 1,950 1{,}950 validation conditions across 30 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8 % 45.8\% and
the transport energy score by 26.1 % 26.1\% relative to training with mean
squared error alone. Both measures improve for every stock.
These findings support incorporating price geometry and volume into
generative modeling, with field accuracy and predictive uncertainty
evaluated together.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Liquidity in limit-order-book (LOB) markets is dynamic: trading over a finite horizon depends on incoming liquidity as well as the orders currently resting in the book. Models of optimal execution show that liquidity replenishment rates affect trading schedules and execution costs ( Obizhaeva and Wang, 2013 ) . Empirical studies document state-dependent limit-order submissions and the recovery of liquidity following trades and cancellations ( Biais et al., 1995 ; Lo and Hall, 2015 ) . Moreover, estimated quote responses to incoming limit orders vary with their size and price aggressiveness, highlighting the importance of both submitted volume and price placement ( Hautsch and Huang, 2012 ) . A forecast of the book at the end of a horizon, however, does not separately identify the new volume submitted during that interval, because submissions can be offset by cancellations and executions. These observations motivate forecasting how much new limit-order volume will arrive and where it will be submitted, as one component of the future trading environment. Forecasting future order supply requires characterizing uncertainty in both submitted volume and its price allocation. Empirical order-flow analysis documents interdependence between order sizes and arrival dynamics ( Rambaldi et al., 2017 ) . A single expected submission profile cannot express this uncertainty: two predictive distributions can have the same mean field while assigning different probabilities to low submitted volume within a given price region. This motivates representing forecasts as predictive distributions, rather than point predictions alone ( Gneiting et al., 2007 ) . Moreover, marginal distributions at individual prices do not determine how volumes vary jointly across prices and sides; constructing multivariate forecast scenarios requires accounting for dependence as well as the marginal distributions ( Schefzik et al., 2013 ) . Total-volume forecasts omit price allocation, whereas unit-mass price profiles discard absolute volume. We therefore seek a conditional joint distribution over unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, allowing total side volumes, price-localized submissions, and bid–ask submission asymmetries to be examined within the same generated scenarios. Specifically, we model the conditional joint distribution of bid and ask limit-order submission fields over the next five minutes, given the current LOB snapshot and recent order flow. Using both book state and flow history is consistent with queue-reactive Hawkes models that explicitly combine these sources of information ( Wu et al., 2019 ) . Each field coordinate records the cumulative volume of new limit orders submitted on one side within a price bin during the forecast window. We fix the price grid relative to the mid-price observed at the forecast origin and retain absolute submitted volume without unit-mass normalization. Unlike message-level generators coupled to a book simulator ( Nagy et al., 2023 ) , our target aggregates submissions without retaining event order. Since order-book dynamics also involve cancellations and executions ( Huang et al., 2015 ) , the submission fields alone do not determine the subsequent book state or remaining liquidity. We therefore position this conditional order-supply model as a potential component of a financial world model, rather than as a complete simulator of order-book evolution. Learning these submission fields calls for an objective sensitive to both price displacement and differences in submitted volume. We use a conditional diffusion model with a denoising mean squared error (MSE) objective ( Ho et al., 2020 ) . This objective penalizes errors coordinatewise, without explicitly assigning costs to displacement between price levels. Optimal transport provides a geometry-aware comparison by matching mass across locations according to a ground cost ( Feydy et al., 2019 ) . However, balanced transport requires equal total mass, whereas predicted and observed submission fields can have different total volumes. Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) relaxes the marginal constraints through divergence penalties, allowing spatial displacement and mass discrepancies to be considered jointly ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) . We therefore augment diffusion MSE with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence on decoded denoised fields, introducing an auxiliary training signal that explicitly accounts for price placement and unequal submitted volume. Evaluating these forecasts requires assessing not only discrepancies between generated and observed fields, but also the quality of the predictive distribution. Comparisons of market statistics, such as those included in LOB-Bench ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) , provide useful measures of realism, but agreement on selected summaries alone does not determine the conditional joint distribution of submission fields. Even when full fields are compared, averaging distances from individual generated samples to the realization can favor overly concentrated forecasts rather than faithful representations of uncertainty ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . Proper scoring rules instead evaluate predictive distributions and are optimized in expectation by the data-generating distribution ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . We therefore combine mass-aware full-field transport comparisons with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics ( Gneiting et al., 2007 ) , evaluating forecasts against their corresponding realizations at matched forecast origins and horizons. To address this task, we introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for the joint generation of unnormalized bid and ask limit-order submission fields, together with a training objective and evaluation framework tailored to price allocation, submitted volume, and predictive uncertainty. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We incorporate an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary objective into conditional diffusion training. A debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence on decoded denoised fields augments the diffusion mean squared error (MSE), providing a field-level training signal that explicitly accounts for price displacement and differences in total submitted volume. (2) We construct a full-field evaluation framework that combines a mass-aware transport cost with transport and joint-field energy scores, the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for side volumes, and calibration diagnostics. These complementary measures assess field accuracy and predictive uncertainty at matched forecast origins and horizons. (3) We compare MSE-only and MSE+UOT training with statistical baselines across 1,950 1{,}950 forecast conditions from 30 30 U.S. equities, reporting pooled and per-stock results. We examine accuracy–diversity tradeoffs and volume calibration in a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) fine-tuned variant, and assess a larger training configuration that jointly increases model capacity, training data, and optimization budget. Across 1,950 validation conditions on 30 U.S. equities, Base-UOT lowers full-field transport cost by 45.8 % 45.8\% and transport energy score by 26.1 % 26.1\% versus Base-MSE, with both improving for every stock. Joint-field energy and log-side-volume CRPS also improve. The evaluated GRPO configuration further improves transport energy and volume CRPS but worsens full-field cost, joint-field energy, and pooled volume-rank calibration while reducing ensemble dispersion, highlighting trade-offs across distributional metrics.

sections.heading: Market simulation and conditional order-flow generation.
sections.text: Market simulation relies on a model of the order flow that drives changes in liquidity. Agent-based platforms such as ABIDES generate this flow through interactions among trading agents and an exchange ( Byrd et al., 2020 ) , while queue-reactive models specify event intensities conditional on book state ( Huang et al., 2015 ) . Learning aggregate trading behavior directly from historical data provides a complementary approach, as in the conditional generators Stock-GAN and World Agent ( Li et al., 2020 ; Coletta et al., 2022 ) . Autoregressive models learn the corresponding message sequences ( Nagy et al., 2023 ) , and MarS integrates order and order-batch generation within an interactive simulator ( Li et al., 2025 ) . At the level of book states, DiffVolume uses conditional diffusion to generate future resting-volume snapshots ( Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) . Our work addresses future liquidity provision through the conditional generation of new limit-order volume accumulated at each price over a five-minute window. Given the observed book and recent flow, the model produces fields that preserve price placement and total submitted volume while abstracting from within-window event sequences.

sections.heading: Optimal transport for generative training.
sections.text: Optimal transport incorporates the geometry of the data into distributional comparisons through a ground cost ( Peyré and Cuturi, 2019 ) . Entropic regularization makes these comparisons computationally tractable, enabling generative models to be trained with Sinkhorn-based losses ( Genevay et al., 2018 ) . For sequential data, COT-GAN further imposes causal constraints on transport couplings to respect temporal structure ( Xu et al., 2020 ) . These approaches compare distributions of generated and observed samples. Our training objective applies transport within each prediction–target pair, treating submitted volumes as measures supported on the price grid. Because total submitted volume varies across fields, this comparison motivates an unbalanced formulation that accommodates unequal mass ( Piccoli and Rossi, 2014 ) . Debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergences provide differentiable losses for this setting ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) . We incorporate such a divergence as an auxiliary objective alongside the diffusion denoising loss, making training sensitive to both price displacement and volume mismatch.

sections.heading: Market realism and predictive-distribution evaluation.
sections.text: Market simulators are commonly evaluated by their ability to reproduce stylized facts of returns and order-book dynamics ( Cont, 2001 ; Vyetrenko et al., 2020 ) . LOB-Bench formalizes this approach through L 1 L_{1} and Wasserstein-1 comparisons of conditional and unconditional market-statistic distributions, complemented by a learned discriminator and event-response diagnostics ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) . Agreement on selected scalar summaries alone does not determine the joint distribution of volume across prices. We complement these diagnostics by comparing complete, unnormalized submission fields at matched forecast boundaries, with a transport-plus-volume cost that retains price geometry and total volume. A low average cost across generated draws, however, can favor concentrated forecasts without correctly representing predictive uncertainty. Proper scoring rules provide a principled basis for evaluating the predictive distribution ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) , and fair ensemble estimators account for finite sampling ( Ferro, 2014 ) . We therefore pair the field cost with transport and joint-field energy scores, supplemented by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and rank diagnostics for total volume. Section 5 specifies the support and propriety conditions for each score.

sections.heading: Reward-based diffusion fine-tuning.
sections.text: Denoising diffusion policy optimization (DDPO) treats iterative denoising as a sequential decision process, enabling policy-gradient updates from rewards assigned to generated samples ( Black et al., 2024 ) . Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), introduced for mathematical reasoning in language models, estimates advantages from rewards normalized within groups of outputs sampled under the same condition ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . DanceGRPO applies this approach to diffusion and rectified-flow models for image and video generation ( Xue et al., 2025 ) . We apply group-relative fine-tuning to conditional order-flow generation, using a reward that combines price displacement, volume error, and diversity among generated fields. Our evaluation examines whether improvements under the training reward extend to distributional accuracy and volume calibration.

sections.heading: 3. Problem Formulation and Data Representation
sections.text: We study the conditional distribution of new limit-order volume submitted during the next time window. The prediction target is a pair of volume-at-price fields, one for each side of the book, conditioned on an observed book snapshot and recent order flow.

sections.heading: 5. Full-Field and Distributional Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate both the accuracy of individual submission fields and the quality of their predictive distribution. At forecast boundary τ k \tau_{k} , independent model draws A ^ k ( 1 ) , … , A ^ k ( R ) \widehat{A}_{k}^{(1)},\ldots,\widehat{A}_{k}^{(R)} are compared with the realization A k + A_{k}^{+} . These paired field comparisons complement summary-statistic benchmarks such as LOB-Bench ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) . All comparisons retain share volumes and the full supplied price support, including realized flow outside the model’s grid. A common price translation leaves the scores unchanged, so absolute ticks and the shared mid-relative frame give identical values. Table 1 summarizes the eight quantities; sampling and reporting follow Section 6.4 .

sections.heading: 5.1. Full-Field Accuracy
sections.text: For generic bid–ask fields U , V U,V , write j = p / θ ∈ ℤ j=p/\theta\in\mathbb{Z} for the price tick and M s ​ ( U ) = ∑ j U s ​ ( j ) M_{s}(U)=\sum_{j}U_{s}(j) for side mass. When this mass is positive, let F U , s F_{U,s} be the CDF of U s / M s ​ ( U ) U_{s}/M_{s}(U) . The one-dimensional Wasserstein shape discrepancy is (13) w s ​ ( U , V ) = ∑ j ∈ ℤ | F U , s ​ ( j ) − F V , s ​ ( j ) | . w_{s}(U,V)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}\big|F_{U,s}(j)-F_{V,s}(j)\big|. This exact CDF expression measures price displacement in ticks without a transport solver ( Santambrogio, 2015 ) . Normalization removes total volume, so fields with the same shape have zero discrepancy even when their masses differ. To retain both placement and volume, set m s = M s ​ ( U ) m_{s}=M_{s}(U) and n s = M s ​ ( V ) n_{s}=M_{s}(V) and define (14) d full , s ​ ( U , V ) \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{full},s}(U,V) = min ⁡ ( m s , n s ) ​ w s ​ ( U , V ) + λ ​ | m s − n s | , \displaystyle=\min(m_{s},n_{s})\,w_{s}(U,V)+\lambda|m_{s}-n_{s}|, (15) d full ​ ( U , V ) \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{full}}(U,V) = ∑ s d full , s ​ ( U , V ) . \displaystyle=\sum_{s}d_{\mathrm{full},s}(U,V). The first term transports the common mass between the normalized shapes; the second charges for residual volume. With λ = 50 \lambda=50 ticks, the cost has units of share ⋅ \cdot ticks. An equal-mass displacement by δ \delta ticks costs m s ​ | δ | m_{s}|\delta| ; a volume change at fixed shape incurs the mass penalty. If either mass is zero, the transport term is defined as zero, leaving d full , s = λ ​ | m s − n s | d_{\mathrm{full},s}=\lambda|m_{s}-n_{s}| . This feasible plan leaves total marginal defect | m s − n s | |m_{s}-n_{s}| , so its cost upper-bounds unbalanced OT with a λ \lambda -weighted L 1 L^{1} penalty on each marginal discrepancy ( Piccoli and Rossi, 2014 ) . It need not attain the optimal transport value or satisfy the triangle inequality. It also differs from the entropic, KL-relaxed training objective in ( 8 ).

sections.heading: 5.2. Predictive Distribution Quality
sections.text: Averaging field costs over draws measures sample fidelity but does not identify the predictive law: concentrated forecasts can achieve small average errors. Proper scoring rules instead attain their minimum expected value at the true conditional law; strict propriety makes that minimizer unique ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . For a fixed condition, write U ( r ) = A ^ k ( r ) U^{(r)}=\widehat{A}_{k}^{(r)} and V = A k + V=A_{k}^{+} . Given a ground distance ρ \rho and R ≥ 2 R\geq 2 independent draws, the fair energy-score estimator is ( Ferro, 2014 ) ES ^ ρ \displaystyle\widehat{\mathrm{ES}}_{\rho} = 1 R ​ ∑ r = 1 R ρ ⁡ ( U ( r ) , V ) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\rho(U^{(r)},V) (16) − 1 2 ​ R ​ ( R − 1 ) ∑ r ≠ r ′ ρ ( U ( r ) , U ( r ′ ) ) . \displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{2R(R-1)}\sum_{r\neq r^{\prime}}\rho(U^{(r)},U^{(r^{\prime})}). The pairwise sum uses ordered pairs; independence makes the estimator unbiased for the population score. We retain the mean target distance T ρ T_{\rho} and mean distance between distinct draws D ρ D_{\rho} , so ES ^ ρ = T ρ − D ρ / 2 \widehat{\mathrm{ES}}_{\rho}=T_{\rho}-D_{\rho}/2 .

sections.heading: Transport energy score.
sections.text: To combine price geometry with volume uncertainty, set g s ​ ( U ) = log ⁡ ( 1 + M s ​ ( U ) ) g_{s}(U)=\log(1+M_{s}(U)) and use (17) ρ T ​ ( U , V ) = 1 2 ​ ∑ s [ w s ​ ( U , V ) κ + β ​ | g s ​ ( U ) − g s ​ ( V ) | ] , \rho_{T}(U,V)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\left[\frac{w_{s}(U,V)}{\kappa}+\beta\big|g_{s}(U)-g_{s}(V)\big|\right], with κ = 50 \kappa=50 ticks and β = 1 \beta=1 . The symmetric log-mass term reduces the dominance of large volumes without exact scale invariance. On laws with nonempty sides and finite first metric moments, ES T \mathrm{ES}_{T} is proper because ρ T \rho_{T} is a sum of L 1 L^{1} distances and hence of negative type ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ; Székely and Rizzo, 2013 ) . Its additive side, shape, and mass terms do not identify their dependence, so it is not strictly proper for the joint field law. The GRPO reward in ( 12 ) uses a different mass discrepancy and does not inherit this propriety claim. For each side, the target and all draws must be either all nonempty or all empty; the latter receives zero score. Both side scores must be defined. Mixed empty/nonempty ensembles are excluded, and the propriety statement does not extend to laws mixing empty and nonempty fields.

sections.heading: Joint-field energy score.
sections.text: To assess the joint bid–ask law, define z s ​ ( U ) ​ ( j ) = log ⁡ ( 1 + U s ​ ( j ) ) z_{s}(U)(j)=\log(1+U_{s}(j)) and (18) ρ 2 ​ ( U , V ) = [ 1 2 ​ B ​ ∑ s ∑ j ∈ ℤ ( z s ​ ( U ) ​ ( j ) − z s ​ ( V ) ​ ( j ) ) 2 ] 1 / 2 . \rho_{2}(U,V)=\left[\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{s}\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}\big(z_{s}(U)(j)-z_{s}(V)(j)\big)^{2}\right]^{1/2}. Here B = 10001 B=10001 fixes normalization without truncating support, and the log transform uses raw shares without model-specific standardization. The injective log-field map lies in a separable Hilbert space, whose norm distance has strong negative type ( Lyons, 2013 ) . Thus the resulting ES 2 \mathrm{ES}_{2} is strictly proper for the joint field law under finite first metric moments, including laws with empty fields. Its binwise geometry complements transport: the penalty for moving an isolated spike to another bin does not increase with the distance moved.

sections.heading: 6.1. Data and Experimental Splits
sections.text: We use LOBSTER full-depth order-message data for a fixed panel of 30 30 U.S. equities. 1 1 1 AAPL, AMGN, AMZN, AXP, BA, CAT, CRM, CSCO, CVX, DIS, GS, HD, HON, IBM, JNJ, JPM, KO, MCD, MMM, MRK, MSFT, NKE, NVDA, PG, SHW, TRV, UNH, V, VZ, and WMT. Each session is restricted to 10:30–16:00 Eastern Time, with a common one-cent price lattice. We construct the contemporaneous-snapshot (lag0) conditions of Section 3 : the book snapshot and preceding five minutes of submission flow condition the forecast of bid and ask submission fields over the next Δ ​ w = 300 \Delta w=300 seconds. The Base models train on 10 10 trading days from June 8–22, 2026. The Large models extend this split with 19 19 earlier days from May 11–June 5, giving 29 29 training days in total. Training uses window-grid offsets of 0 0 , 60 60 , 120 120 , 180 180 , and 240 240 seconds, yielding 96,300 96{,}300 Base and 279,270 279{,}270 Large training pairs. Volume-transform and summary-feature statistics are fitted separately for each training split using only its unshifted windows. All models are compared on a fixed corpus from June 23, 2026 containing 1,950 1{,}950 conditions, with 65 65 per stock. Evaluation uses the unshifted grid, with target windows starting at 10:35 through 15:55 Eastern Time. This day also serves for checkpoint selection, so the reported results are validation-set comparisons following chronological training. June 24 is reserved in the configured test split and is not used in these comparisons. The same 30 30 stocks appear in training and evaluation; per-stock results characterize performance variation across this observed panel.

sections.heading: 6.2. Experimental Comparisons and Baselines
sections.text: The primary comparison uses three Base variants of the conditional diffusion model in Section 4.1 . Base-MSE trains with the diffusion MSE in ( 7 ); Base-UOT adds the transport auxiliary objective in ( 10 ). Throughout, UOT denotes this combined MSE+UOT objective. Base-GRPO fine-tunes Base-UOT as described in Section 4.4 . These variants examine how the training objective and fine-tuning procedure affect field accuracy and predictive uncertainty, alongside the statistical references below. An expanded configuration adds Large-MSE and Large-UOT to check whether the MSE/UOT findings persist with greater capacity, more data, and longer training (Section 6.3 ). Two parametric baselines fit the observed submission field A k − A_{k}^{-} . Skew-normal fits one skew-normal distribution per side, using volume weights within 50 50 ticks of that side’s modal price. Skew-normal mixture fits the full observed support, with BIC selecting one or two components per side ( K max = 2 K_{\max}=2 ) and observed share volume as the effective sample size. Both fit separately at each forecast boundary and scale the fitted shape to the observed side’s total volume, yielding a deterministic forecast field. They use recent flow without book-depth conditioning; their comparison includes differences in fitting support and component limits. For a historical distributional reference, Empirical samples complete bid–ask fields from the same instrument and five-minute window index on the Base configuration’s 10 10 training days, using unshifted windows only. Each selected field is translated from its own snapshot-mid anchor to the current anchor. Draws are uniform and independent with replacement. This baseline uses instrument identity, time of day, and the snapshot anchor; it does not use recent flow or book depth.

sections.heading: Diffusion training.
sections.text: Base has 58.7 58.7 M parameters (hidden width d = 512 d=512 , 12 12 blocks, 8 8 heads) and trains for 30,000 30{,}000 steps at learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} ; Large uses 174.3 174.3 M parameters ( d = 768 d=768 , 16 16 blocks, 12 12 heads) and 100,000 100{,}000 steps at 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Within each size, MSE and UOT share architecture, data, and optimizer settings. Both use AdamW with constant learning rates, batch size 64 64 , weight decay 0.01 0.01 , gradient-norm clipping at 1 1 , mixed precision, and EMA decay 0.9999 0.9999 . Both sizes use patch width P = 16 P=16 , feed-forward width 4 ​ d 4d , and dropout 0.1 0.1 ; the grid, diffusion schedule, and UOT coefficients are also shared. Each learned configuration uses one training seed, 42 42 .

sections.heading: GRPO fine-tuning.
sections.text: Base-GRPO starts from the selected Base-UOT EMA weights and uses the same training split. Each of 500 500 iterations samples G = 8 G=8 fields for each of 16 16 conditions, followed by one policy-update epoch. Updates use AdamW with learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , zero weight decay, gradient-norm clipping at 1 1 , mixed precision, and EMA decay 0.99 0.99 . The policy-ratio clipping threshold is 0.2 0.2 and the KL-penalty coefficient is 0.02 0.02 .

sections.heading: 6.4. Evaluation and Reporting Protocol
sections.text: All models are evaluated on the common lag0 corpus in Section 6.1 , with matched forecast boundaries and realized targets. Their conditioning inputs follow Section 6.2 .

sections.heading: Forecast generation.
sections.text: Diffusion models generate R = 4 R=4 independent fields per condition from selected EMA weights (evaluation base seed 0 0 ). MSE/UOT use 50 50 DDIM steps ( η = 0 \eta=0 ); Base-GRPO uses its 20 20 -step training sampler ( η = 1 \eta=1 ). Empirical also draws four independent fields; each skew-normal baseline is deterministic ( R = 1 R=1 ). Base/Large share the 50 50 -step sampler, whereas the GRPO comparison combines fine-tuning and a sampler change.

sections.heading: Scoring and calibration.
sections.text: Fields in shares are scored against full-support targets, including realized flow outside the model grid, using the eight quantities in Section 5 . Field costs and errors average over defined draws; distributional scores use the ensemble jointly. Deterministic R = 1 R=1 forecasts have zero inter-draw terms, leaving only target distance. For GRPO, we retain both energy scores’ target and inter-draw components. Volume calibration compares R = 4 R=4 models using RI and interior-rank coverage (nominal 0.6 0.6 ). Ties are broken uniformly at random using reproducible sample-based seeds.

sections.heading: Aggregation and reporting.
sections.text: Sided W 1 W_{1} and NTVE average defined draws within sides, then equally across sides, requiring both means. Full-field cost sums sides; log-field MSE follows ( 18 ). Per-stock and pooled means equally weight defined boundaries, with per-metric valid and excluded counts; volume ranks pool boundary–side pairs. Raw costs can be dominated by high-volume windows and are interpreted alongside shape and relative- or log-volume metrics. Comparisons are descriptive, using the checkpoint-selection day and one training seed per learned configuration.

sections.heading: 7. Results
sections.text: We assess field accuracy and predictive-distribution quality on the common 1,950 1{,}950 lag0 conditions across 30 30 stocks described in Section 6.1 . All field costs and distributional scores are defined on every condition for the eight selected models, with no exclusions. Volume-rank diagnostics use 3,900 3{,}900 condition–side pairs per model. As specified in Section 6.4 , these are descriptive comparisons on the checkpoint-selection day, with one training seed per learned configuration.

sections.heading: 7.3. Expanded Training Configuration
sections.text: The UOT advantage over MSE in full-field cost and both energy scores persists in the expanded configuration. Relative to Base-UOT, Large-UOT reduces full-field cost by 2.1 % 2.1\% and ES T \mathrm{ES}_{T} by 17.5 % 17.5\% . Large-MSE nevertheless retains lower NTVE and log-field MSE than Large-UOT. Capacity, training data, optimizer steps, and learning rate change together, so this comparison does not isolate their individual effects.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
sections.text: We presented OrderFlowDiT for conditional generation of unnormalized limit-order submission fields, together with an evaluation framework that assesses price placement, total volume, and predictive uncertainty. On 1,950 1{,}950 validation conditions across 30 30 U.S. equities, Base-UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8 % 45.8\% and the transport energy score by 26.1 % 26.1\% relative to Base-MSE, with gains in both measures for every stock. The UOT advantage persists when model capacity, training data, and optimization budget increase together. The GRPO variant illustrates the need for complementary distributional diagnostics: its lower transport energy score coexists with reduced sample diversity, a worse joint-field score, and weaker volume calibration. These results support training and evaluation that account jointly for price geometry, submitted volume, and the distribution of possible outcomes. The central limitation is that generating submission flow does not complete a financial world model. An impact model is also needed to connect the current book, order flow, and trading actions to the distribution of subsequent book states and prices. Our aggregated fields omit cancellations, executions, and event ordering, so they cannot by themselves determine these transitions. Learning and validating this link, including the market’s response to trading actions, is the next step toward multi-step simulation and the evaluation of trading decisions.

We study the conditional distribution of limit-order volume submitted over the next five minutes, given the current order book and recent order flow. The task requires capturing price placement, total volume, and predictive uncertainty jointly. Coordinate-wise diffusion losses do not explicitly account for price displacement, while normalizing fields to unit mass removes information about total volume. Agreement on selected summary statistics also does not establish fidelity to the joint field distribution. We introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary loss. We also develop a full-field evaluation framework that combines a transport cost sensitive to price placement and total volume with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics. In the primary comparison on 1,950 1{,}950 validation conditions across 30 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8 % 45.8\% and the transport energy score by 26.1 % 26.1\% relative to training with mean squared error alone. Both measures improve for every stock. These findings support incorporating price geometry and volume into generative modeling, with field accuracy and predictive uncertainty evaluated together. Keywords: limit order book, world model, generative models, optimal transport, evaluation, market microstructure 1. Introduction Liquidity in limit-order-book (LOB) markets is dynamic: trading over a finite horizon depends on incoming liquidity as well as the orders currently resting in the book. Models of optimal execution show that liquidity replenishment rates affect trading schedules and execution costs ( Obizhaeva and Wang, 2013 ) . Empirical studies document state-dependent limit-order submissions and the recovery of liquidity following trades and cancellations ( Biais et al., 1995 ; Lo and Hall, 2015 ) . Moreover, estimated quote responses to incoming limit orders vary with their size and price aggressiveness, highlighting the importance of both submitted volume and price placement ( Hautsch and Huang, 2012 ) . A forecast of the book at the end of a horizon, however, does not separately identify the new volume submitted during that interval, because submissions can be offset by cancellations and executions. These observations motivate forecasting how much new limit-order volume will arrive and where it will be submitted, as one component of the future trading environment. Forecasting future order supply requires characterizing uncertainty in both submitted volume and its price allocation. Empirical order-flow analysis documents interdependence between order sizes and arrival dynamics ( Rambaldi et al., 2017 ) . A single expected submission profile cannot express this uncertainty: two predictive distributions can have the same mean field while assigning different probabilities to low submitted volume within a given price region. This motivates representing forecasts as predictive distributions, rather than point predictions alone ( Gneiting et al., 2007 ) . Moreover, marginal distributions at individual prices do not determine how volumes vary jointly across prices and sides; constructing multivariate forecast scenarios requires accounting for dependence as well as the marginal distributions ( Schefzik et al., 2013 ) . Total-volume forecasts omit price allocation, whereas unit-mass price profiles discard absolute volume. We therefore seek a conditional joint distribution over unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, allowing total side volumes, price-localized submissions, and bid–ask submission asymmetries to be examined within the same generated scenarios. Specifically, we model the conditional joint distribution of bid and ask limit-order submission fields over the next five minutes, given the current LOB snapshot and recent order flow. Using both book state and flow history is consistent with queue-reactive Hawkes models that explicitly combine these sources of information ( Wu et al., 2019 ) . Each field coordinate records the cumulative volume of new limit orders submitted on one side within a price bin during the forecast window. We fix the price grid relative to the mid-price observed at the forecast origin and retain absolute submitted volume without unit-mass normalization. Unlike message-level generators coupled to a book simulator ( Nagy et al., 2023 ) , our target aggregates submissions without retaining event order. Since order-book dynamics also involve cancellations and executions ( Huang et al., 2015 ) , the submission fields alone do not determine the subsequent book state or remaining liquidity. We therefore position this conditional order-supply model as a potential component of a financial world model, rather than as a complete simulator of order-book evolution. Learning these submission fields calls for an objective sensitive to both price displacement and differences in submitted volume. We use a conditional diffusion model with a denoising mean squared error (MSE) objective ( Ho et al., 2020 ) . This objective penalizes errors coordinatewise, without explicitly assigning costs to displacement between price levels. Optimal transport provides a geometry-aware comparison by matching mass across locations according to a ground cost ( Feydy et al., 2019 ) . However, balanced transport requires equal total mass, whereas predicted and observed submission fields can have different total volumes. Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) relaxes the marginal constraints through divergence penalties, allowing spatial displacement and mass discrepancies to be considered jointly ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) . We therefore augment diffusion MSE with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence on decoded denoised fields, introducing an auxiliary training signal that explicitly accounts for price placement and unequal submitted volume. Evaluating these forecasts requires assessing not only discrepancies between generated and observed fields, but also the quality of the predictive distribution. Comparisons of market statistics, such as those included in LOB-Bench ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) , provide useful measures of realism, but agreement on selected summaries alone does not determine the conditional joint distribution of submission fields. Even when full fields are compared, averaging distances from individual generated samples to the realization can favor overly concentrated forecasts rather than faithful representations of uncertainty ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . Proper scoring rules instead evaluate predictive distributions and are optimized in expectation by the data-generating distribution ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . We therefore combine mass-aware full-field transport comparisons with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics ( Gneiting et al., 2007 ) , evaluating forecasts against their corresponding realizations at matched forecast origins and horizons. To address this task, we introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for the joint generation of unnormalized bid and ask limit-order submission fields, together with a training objective and evaluation framework tailored to price allocation, submitted volume, and predictive uncertainty. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We incorporate an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary objective into conditional diffusion training. A debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence on decoded denoised fields augments the diffusion mean squared error (MSE), providing a field-level training signal that explicitly accounts for price displacement and differences in total submitted volume. (2) We construct a full-field evaluation framework that combines a mass-aware transport cost with transport and joint-field energy scores, the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for side volumes, and calibration diagnostics. These complementary measures assess field accuracy and predictive uncertainty at matched forecast origins and horizons. (3) We compare MSE-only and MSE+UOT training with statistical baselines across 1,950 1{,}950 forecast conditions from 30 30 U.S. equities, reporting pooled and per-stock results. We examine accuracy–diversity tradeoffs and volume calibration in a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) fine-tuned variant, and assess a larger training configuration that jointly increases model capacity, training data, and optimization budget. Across 1,950 validation conditions on 30 U.S. equities, Base-UOT lowers full-field transport cost by 45.8 % 45.8\% and transport energy score by 26.1 % 26.1\% versus Base-MSE, with both improving for every stock. Joint-field energy and log-side-volume CRPS also improve. The evaluated GRPO configuration further improves transport energy and volume CRPS but worsens full-field cost, joint-field energy, and pooled volume-rank calibration while reducing ensemble dispersion, highlighting trade-offs across distributional metrics. 2. Related Work Market simulation and conditional order-flow generation. Market simulation relies on a model of the order flow that drives changes in liquidity. Agent-based platforms such as ABIDES generate this flow through interactions among trading agents and an exchange ( Byrd et al., 2020 ) , while queue-reactive models specify event intensities conditional on book state ( Huang et al., 2015 ) . Learning aggregate trading behavior directly from historical data provides a complementary approach, as in the conditional generators Stock-GAN and World Agent ( Li et al., 2020 ; Coletta et al., 2022 ) . Autoregressive models learn the corresponding message sequences ( Nagy et al., 2023 ) , and MarS integrates order and order-batch generation within an interactive simulator ( Li et al., 2025 ) . At the level of book states, DiffVolume uses conditional diffusion to generate future resting-volume snapshots ( Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) . Our work addresses future liquidity provision through the conditional generation of new limit-order volume accumulated at each price over a five-minute window. Given the observed book and recent flow, the model produces fields that preserve price placement and total submitted volume while abstracting from within-window event sequences. Optimal transport for generative training. Optimal transport incorporates the geometry of the data into distributional comparisons through a ground cost ( Peyré and Cuturi, 2019 ) . Entropic regularization makes these comparisons computationally tractable, enabling generative models to be trained with Sinkhorn-based losses ( Genevay et al., 2018 ) . For sequential data, COT-GAN further imposes causal constraints on transport couplings to respect temporal structure ( Xu et al., 2020 ) . These approaches compare distributions of generated and observed samples. Our training objective applies transport within each prediction–target pair, treating submitted volumes as measures supported on the price grid. Because total submitted volume varies across fields, this comparison motivates an unbalanced formulation that accommodates unequal mass ( Piccoli and Rossi, 2014 ) . Debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergences provide differentiable losses for this setting ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) . We incorporate such a divergence as an auxiliary objective alongside the diffusion denoising loss, making training sensitive to both price displacement and volume mismatch. Market realism and predictive-distribution evaluation. Market simulators are commonly evaluated by their ability to reproduce stylized facts of returns and order-book dynamics ( Cont, 2001 ; Vyetrenko et al., 2020 ) . LOB-Bench formalizes this approach through L 1 L_{1} and Wasserstein-1 comparisons of conditional and unconditional market-statistic distributions, complemented by a learned discriminator and event-response diagnostics ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) . Agreement on selected scalar summaries alone does not determine the joint distribution of volume across prices. We complement these diagnostics by comparing complete, unnormalized submission fields at matched forecast boundaries, with a transport-plus-volume cost that retains price geometry and total volume. A low average cost across generated draws, however, can favor concentrated forecasts without correctly representing predictive uncertainty. Proper scoring rules provide a principled basis for evaluating the predictive distribution ( Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) , and fair ensemble estimators account for finite sampling ( Ferro, 2014 ) . We therefore pair the field cost with transport and joint-field energy scores, supplemented by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and rank diagnostics for total volume. Section 5 specifies the support and propriety conditions for each score. Reward-based diffusion fine-tuning. Denoising diffusion policy optimization (DDPO) treats iterative denoising as a sequential decision process, enabling policy-gradient updates from rewards assigned to generated samples ( Black et al., 2024 ) . Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), introduced for mathematical reasoning in language models, estimates advantages from rewards normalized within groups of outputs sampled under the same condition ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . DanceGRPO applies this approach to diffusion and rectified-flow models for image and video generation ( Xue et al., 2025 ) . We apply group-relative fine-tuning to conditional order-flow generation, using a reward that combines price displacement, volume error, and diversity among generated fields. Our evaluation examines whether improvements under the training reward extend to distributional accuracy and volume calibration. 3.
